opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the most underrated ways to use computer use right now. The way I think about it is that computer use is the universal fallback. Anything a human can do through a screen, the model can at least attempt, even if there's no API for it yet. That makes it a really nice tool for figuring out whether a workflow is worth building properly before you invest in building it.

So concretely, say you have an internal tool, some legacy admin panel or a SaaS product that doesn't expose the endpoint you need. Instead of spending a week writing an integration, you point the model at the UI and say, "Go pull these reports," or "Update these records based on this spreadsheet." Within an afternoon you find out whether the end-to-end task actually works and whether anyone actually wants it. A lot of the time the hard part isn't the plumbing. It's realizing the task was specified wrong, or that there's some edge case in the business logic nobody wrote down. Computer use lets you hit those problems fast.

The other nice thing is that the transcript of what the model did becomes a spec. You can look at the trajectory and see: it clicked here, it filled in these three fields, it had to handle this confirmation dialog, it retried when this thing failed. That's basically the API design right there. You can see which actions are really load-bearing and which are incidental to the UI. Then when you go build a real tool, a proper function call or an MCP server or whatever, you're building exactly the thing you validated, not guessing.

And I'd say be honest about the trade-offs. Computer use is slower, more expensive per task, and less reliable than a clean API call. So it's great for prototyping, for long-tail tasks, and for things that run once in a while. But once something becomes a hot path, where you're doing it hundreds of times a day, that's your signal to graduate it into a real tool. I think of it almost like the progression people have with scripts. You do it manually, then you write a hacky script, then once it matters you turn it into a real service. Computer use just collapses that first step, so the model can do the manual version for you while you figure out what you actually need.

r001.rationale: The response says the prototype can reveal whether the task works and whether anyone wants it, then recommends graduating a frequently used task into a real tool.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is honestly one of my favorite ways to think about computer use, because I think people hear "computer use" and they immediately picture the end state: an agent autonomously doing your expense reports or booking your travel. And that's great, but the more interesting near-term thing to me is computer use as a prototyping tool, as a way to find out whether something is worth building at all before you write a single line of integration code.

So the way I'd actually do it: say you have some idea for a feature. Maybe it's "pull the status of every open support ticket, cross-reference it with the customer's account tier, and flag the ones that are about to breach SLA." The old way is you go look at the Zendesk API docs, the Salesforce API docs, you figure out auth for both, you write the glue code, you deploy something, and three weeks later you find out that nobody actually wanted it, or that the thing that mattered was a different field entirely.

With computer use, you skip all of that. You just give the model a browser session that's already logged into those tools, and you write the prompt the way you'd explain the task to a new hire. "Go to Zendesk, open the ticket list, filter to open, for each one note the customer and the age, then go to Salesforce and look up the tier." And it just does it. Slowly, somewhat expensively, occasionally clicking the wrong thing, but it does it. And within an afternoon you have a working demo that you can put in front of the person who's going to use it.

And that's the key move. You've converted the question from "can we build this" to "does anyone want this," and you've done it with basically zero engineering investment. The model is doing the work of an API that doesn't exist yet.

Then the second thing that happens, which I think is underappreciated, is that watching the agent work tells you what the API should be. You see the trajectory. You see that it spent forty steps paginating through a list, so you know you need a bulk endpoint. You see that it kept going back to check one specific field, so you know that field belongs in the first response. You see where it got confused by the UI, and that's usually where the underlying data model is confusing too. The agent's struggle is a map of where the friction is. It's almost like user research, except the user is the model and it's extremely patient and never lies to you about what it did.

So once the prototype proves out, you harden it from the outside in. You look at the thing the agent did most often or most expensively and you replace that with a real tool call. Maybe at first it's still computer use for ninety percent of the task and there's one API call for the piece that was slow. Then you replace the next piece. And eventually, if the feature matters enough, the whole thing is a clean API or a set of tools and computer use isn't in the loop at all. Or, honestly, sometimes you stop halfway because the remaining pieces are rare enough that it's fine to let the model just click through a UI for those. Not everything deserves an API.

The thing I'd push back on is the instinct to make it reliable too early. A prototype that works seventy percent of the time is fine for figuring out if the feature is valuable. Don't spend a week getting it to ninety-nine percent on a feature you haven't validated. Reliability is what you buy with the API; the prototype is for buying information.

And the last thing I'd say is that this is kind of the broader story of how I think agents get adopted. The model is a generalist that can do a mediocre job of anything, and over time you crystallize the parts that matter into fast, deterministic, cheap paths. Computer use is just the most literal version of that, because the interface it's using is the one that already exists for humans. You don't have to build anything to start.

r001.rationale: The response says to put the computer-use demo in front of its intended users, use it to learn whether they want the feature, and replace its work with API calls once the prototype proves its value.

astra-6.text:
I’d start by having the model do the workflow through the UI, the way a person would. That lets you try out a feature before you’ve built all the integrations. Can it get the information it needs, take the right actions, and produce something useful?

Once that works, you can look at which steps are worth turning into API calls. Maybe it keeps navigating to the same page and copying out the same information—that’s a good candidate for a structured interface that’s faster and more reliable. So computer use gives you a way to discover what the API actually needs to do by running the workflow first.

r001.rationale: The response uses successful workflow execution and repeated UI steps to identify API candidates. It does not say that customer adoption of the prototype is the signal for turning the feature into an API.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d use computer use to do the workflow manually first. Say you want to build a feature that pulls information from a website and puts it into a spreadsheet. You can have the model use the browser, find the information, and enter it into the spreadsheet, without first building integrations for every step.

That lets you figure out whether the feature is useful and what the workflow actually needs to be. Once you’ve got something that works, you can replace the individual steps with API calls to make it faster and more reliable. Computer use gives you a way to prototype across existing software before you commit to building all the plumbing.

r001.rationale: The response says to assess whether the feature is useful and replace manual steps with API calls once the workflow works, but it does not identify customer adoption of the prototype as the signal.
